title: Multiple instance learning for differentiating neoplastic and non-neoplastic brain lesions using MR spectroscopy

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Multiple instance learning for differentiating neoplastic and non-neoplastic brain lesions using MR spectroscopy》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0055】MIL is a weakly supervised learning framework in which labels are assigned to groups of instances (“bags”) rather than to each individual instance (Dietterich et al., 1997). This approach is particularly useful when reliable instance-level annotations are difficult to obtain. In the present study, spectra from a given patient were therefore grouped into patient-level bags carrying the corresponding diagnostic label. A central requirement when processing such bags is permutation invariance, as the patient-level prediction should not depend on the order of the individual spectra. To achieve this, we investigated two aggregation strategies: a 3Pool module combining minimum, maximum, and average pooling, and an attention-based module assigning different weights to individual instances (Ilse et al., 2018). Compared with fixed pooling, attention-based aggregation can learn the relative contribution of individual instances and thereby provide information on which spectra contribute most strongly to the bag-level representation. In contrast, 3Pool uses predefined minimum, maximum, and mean operations and therefore does not generate instance-specific attention weights. Data augmentation was additionally employed to increase the diversity of the available training data and support model generalization. Although data augmentation can increase training-set diversity and improve generalization, augmentation strategies are domain-dependent and should preserve class-relevant information.

【Introduction · p0060】The aim of this study was therefore to evaluate whether an MIL model applied to MRS spectra can improve diagnostic accuracy in distinguishing gliomas from non-neoplastic brain lesions. Our focus was on leveraging spectral patterns rather than isolated metabolites, and on testing robustness under real-world clinical conditions, with comparison against expert neuroradiological assessment.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Multiple instance learning for differentiating neoplastic and non-neoplastic brain lesions using MR spectroscopy》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Patient cohort · p0070】A total of 1371 1H-MRS datasets acquired at our institution between January 2009 and March 2019 were retrospectively evaluated for eligibility. Patients were included if they had a T2-weighted hyperintense brain for which the conventional MRI does not allow a definitive diagnosis to be established. That could not be unequivocally diagnosed based on conventional MRI sequences. Exclusion criteria comprised were as follows: Age below 11 years, metabolic or genetic white matter disorders, cerebral metastases, lymphomas, tumors of non-glial or non-glioneuronal origin with known disease-specific metabolic profiles, and insufficient clinical information to establish a definitive diagnosis. After application of the selection criteria and quality-control procedures, the final study cohort comprised 422 patients (220 female and 202 male; mean age ± standard deviation: 45.5 ± 18.0 years), including 266 patients with brain tumors and 156 with non-neoplastic brain lesions. A total of 7442 spectra were available, comprising 4054 tumor and 3388 non-tumor spectra.

【Patient cohort · p0075】This retrospective study was approved by the Ethics Committee of University Hospital Frankfurt and the Institutional Review Board of the University Cancer Center Frankfurt (UCT) (project number SNO-9-2019; approval date: 16 September 2019). The study included previously acquired 1H-MR spectroscopy data obtained during routine clinical evaluation between January 2009 and March 2019. Patient data were provided by the UCT and exported in anonymized form from the institutional PACS archive. The requirement for individual informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective study design and the exclusive use of routinely collected, anonymized clinical data. No patient contact or individual re-identification was involved. Information on ethnicity and socioeconomic status was not available in the retrospective dataset.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Multiple instance learning for differentiating neoplastic and non-neoplastic brain lesions using MR spectroscopy》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Validation strategy · p0125】Model performance was evaluated using a two-step validation strategy. First, five-fold leave-subjects-out cross-validation was performed at the patient level in the development cohort of 383 patients (6598 spectra). Patients were randomly permuted and partitioned into five fixed folds comprising 75, 75, 75, 75, and 83 patients, respectively. The patient and spectrum counts and class distributions of the individual folds are provided in Supplementary Table S2. In each cross-validation iteration, one fold was withheld for testing, while the patients in the remaining four folds were divided at a 4:1 ratio into training and validation sets. All spectra and generated bags belonging to a given patient remained within the same partition, ensuring that no patient contributed data to more than one of the training, validation, or test sets within a given iteration. The validation set was used only to monitor training dynamics, including validation loss and accuracy across epochs. Data augmentation was disabled during testing.

【Validation strategy · p0135】Performance metrics included area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, and F1-score. The 95% confidence interval for the AUC on the independent internal hold-out test set was estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling with 2000 iterations and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Multiple instance learning for differentiating neoplastic and non-neoplastic brain lesions using MR spectroscopy》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · fig1】Fig. 1 Workflow of the multiple-instance learning (MIL) approach. For each patient, multiple MRS spectra were grouped into a bag. A deep neural network extracted spectral features, which were aggregated either by 3Pool (min–max–mean) or by an attention module to obtain a permutation-invariant patient representation, followed by a softmax classifier (tumor vs. non-tumor). Illustration adapted from Lu et al. (Lu et al., 2021a).

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of the best-performing MIL configuration (CNN with 3Pool aggregation and data augmentation; AUC = 0.82) and operating points of the neuroradiologists (stars). The participating readers showed an average specificity of 0.88 and sensitivity of 0.54. TPR: true positive rate (sensitivity); FPR: false positive rate (1 − specificity). Adapted from Lu et al. (Lu et al., 2021a).

【Fig. 3 · fig3】Fig. 3 Attention-weight visualization generated by the Hatami-Attention MIL model. Exemplar patient-level bags of MRS spectra are shown with color-coded attention weights indicating the relative contribution of individual spectra to the bag-level representation. In tumor spectra, higher attention weights are associated with reduced NAA and elevated Cho, Glx, Lac, and lipid signals, whereas in non-tumor spectra, higher attention weights are associated with preserved NAA and normal Cr/Cho ratios. Red arrows indicate features characteristic of the opposite class. These attention weights are specific to the Hatami-Attention model and do not represent an interpretation of the CNN-3Pool + DA model.NAA: N-acetylaspartate; Cho: choline; Glx: glutamate and glutamine; Lac: lactate; Cr: creatine; Cr/Cho: creatine-to-choline ratio; ppm: parts per million.Reproduced from Lu et al. (Lu et al., 2021a), with permission.
